explanation: No shared theme: it fires on a grab-bag of tokens, including word-piece continuations inside compound or technical names (bis-phen-ol, onabot-ulin-um, namen-ode, 22-q), short function words in fixed phrases ('must be', 'go to', 'switching to', 'weak var', 'shakes his head') and code tokens (__asm__). You cannot predict strong firing from either the token or its context.

Fires on word-piece tokens inside proper names that are rare or foreign, especially Latin species epithets (Crataegus la-evigata, X. la-evis, Leontopodium long-ifolium), surnames (Cunha, Upchurch, Munoz, Counsilman) and place names (Chiang Mai, Chonburi), plus legal-citation pieces like 'U.S.C.A'. It is weak on ordinary words. There are a few unrelated hits (End Sub newline, 'You' starting a paragraph).

Fires mostly on month or season names in date positions ("June 9", "July 29,", "in January 201x", "the summer of", "Summer 193x"), most strongly in datelines and bylines. It also fires on assorted capitalized name pieces (Yellow Sea, Nuevo México, Turbo C++) and a few Spanish words, which look like a separate secondary job.

Fires on the first word-piece of a word that the tokenizer splits into fragments, mostly in non-English text (German, Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish) or in unusual names (O'Be-irne, Or-igi, Pr-arthana, B-oggiano, Pot-encier). The marked token is the start or middle of a word whose remaining pieces follow. It is weak on whole common English words.

Fires on boilerplate tokens in code and formal or technical text: '#define' and '#pragma' in C headers, '-exclusive' in 'non-exclusive' license grants, decorators and annotations (@dataclass, @interface), and math-proof wording ('a finite', 'there exists', 'converges uniformly'). These may share a 'formal technical register' feature, but the token types are mixed.

Fires on the separator token right after a namespace or ID prefix in structured markup: the ':' in XML/XAML namespace prefixes (xmlns:android, xsi:schemaLocation, h:form, f:metadata) and the '-' in citation and anchor IDs of scientific articles ([@b16-27], #sec1-ijerph, mrm27594-bib). It is weaker on ordinary chemical or compound hyphens (beta-estradiol).

Mixed. It fires on function words in Portuguese and French ('no', 'en', 'alguns'), on name pieces (Somerville, Monrovia, Carlo), on dots inside version numbers (1.0.2, 7.3.0) and on assorted English words ('like', 'in', 'have'). No single trigger stands out.

Fires on a finite auxiliary or copula verb (was, is, are, am, can, will, would, don't) that begins a predicate whose subject is not stated right before it, typically after 'but' or 'and' with the subject dropped ('...but was given', 'I'm using X and am running'). It also fires after a comma-separated parenthetical or a long subject phrase. Auxiliaries that follow an explicit pronoun subject are weak.

No clear unifying feature. It fires on pieces of legal case numbers and citations (CR-770, S.W.3d, '(Ch)', 'No.'), timestamp digits, '©', and a range of ordinary words in boilerplate web or legal text ('so easy', 'all time high', 'permanently delete', 'many'). Predicting it is hard.

Fires on the content-word token that completes a multi-token term or name, often the last piece of a scientific or proper term (white dwar-fs, neutron star, Robert Mueller, creatine phosphokin-ase, estate plan, bench press). It also fires on the '-' in ZIP+4 codes (02110-1301). Activation is spread across unrelated domains.

Mostly fires on Russian text, especially case endings and word pieces in Cyrillic programming Q&A (больш-ей, мо-ем, было, код-е). It also fires on assorted numeric or identifier tokens in code and config (rfc1034, 0x1c, Ruby200) and on name pieces (Chi Chi, Mead, Mehta). This is a mixture.

Fires on the preposition, verb or punctuation that links a person or statement to the media outlet it is attributed to, i.e. the token right before an outlet name: 'told [Gazzetta]', 'a staff writer for [CBS]', 'in an interview with', 'polled by [Reuters]', 'featured on USA Today, [FOX]', 'developer at [BuzzFeed]', 'of [Country Universe]'. It is weaker for 'according to' and for generic prepositions.

Fires on '=' and '+' operators, and on the token after '=', inside generated algebra word problems ('Suppose -p + d - 10 = -6*p', 'Solve ... = 0 for v'). It fires moderately on the question words of the same math-problem genre and on digits in case or patent numbers, and weakly on '=' in code.

Fires on the separator inside a compact multi-part token sequence, chiefly the '.' between version-number components (1.0.0, 4.6.1, php5.4.3) and the hyphen or slash in compound strings (author-composer-lyricist, Arg-Gly-Asp, top/left/bottom, Design/Build/Fly, S-Q-L). Colons in timestamps count too. Periods after initials are weaker.
